utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. McCloskey: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, remind us both to remain -- try to keep it slow. I know we have a lot to go through. We yesterday had talked about orders briefly. Before moving on, can you tell us what the normal direction and chain of orders is. Where do they go? From what unit to what unit normally?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a general rule, the order chain flows from the higher unit or the higher command to the lower one. At the macro level, the orders would originate from the president of the republic as the supreme commander. We go through the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. It would then be sent to the corps and forwarded to the brigades and battalions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we'll in fact see some orders later on that reflect that. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we've also seen in this case situations where General Mladic appears to be issuing orders directly to brigade commanders. What can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that type of event is -- well, it's not normal. It's certainly not unheard of, either in the structure of the VRS or even in other military structures. General Mladic as the commander of the Main Staff is, in effect, the commander of the army. And it's not unusual for them to give orders to brigade commanders, sometimes bypassing the corps commander. It's not the normal chain of events, but in a situation that requires some expediency, it can be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If a brigade commander receives such an order from Mladic, is he duty-bound to carry it out?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is duty-bound to carry it out. It is considered part of the chain of command. In the normal procedure both envisioned in the regulations and when this issue was discussed with a number of VRS senior officers is that it would be carried out, but that what would occur is that immediately after receiving the order, the brigade commander would take the initiative to ensure that his superior, the corps commander or whatever the skipped commander was would be informed immediately what the order was, to ensure that there was no difficulty with the larger plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've also heard evidence that in this case intelligence or security officers of the corps issued instructions or orders directly to the security officer of a brigade. Is that normal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is normal under what is known in that particular system as a management or professional chain. It is not a chain of command. These individuals -- it's not a higher to lower command relationship. It reflects the relationship where the technical services person, it may be security, it could even be rear services in this case, is charged by the regulations to manage the professional affairs and issues of the lower branch. So in that respect, the orders being passed down is part of the normal chain of communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me give you a particular situation where according to Momir Nikolic he received orders or instructions on the morning of the 12th from a corps security chief Popovic relating to the separation, detention, and execution of the prisoners. How does that fit into this scheme that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that respect, that would be an example of a superior organ, in the case the corps security officer, giving instructions to a brigade security officer in that respect. Those types of orders are given under the general umbrella that the commanders at both the corps and brigade level are already aware of the larger plan and that they're leaving the details of the information of the plan, again be it security or otherwise, to the technical officers at each level who are best equipped to do this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your study of this case and this investigation, have you identified any to indicate that there was a deliberate effort by the Main Staff to cut out any brigade commanders involved in the -- either in the military operation or the operation to murder Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also on that same subject of orders, when a subordinate officer such as the chief of security reports back to his commander about actions that he has carried out pursuant to the orders of another superior, and if that commander remains silent in relation to that report, what if anything does the commander's silence communicate to the subordinate?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. It calls for speculation, Your Honour. I don't think that the gentleman is clairvoyant and can look backwards and say what -- I think an inference can be made, but if there's going to be an inference, I suggest that a more thorough foundation be laid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, we have heard the evidence during the testimonies of the previous witnesses. I think this question is quite clear here. So we also want to know what the witness's conclusions on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Butler, can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And going back to the JNA regulations with respect to command and commanded staff where the commander has the requirement to verify that orders are being carried out, in that particular situation when a subordinate has reported back what orders are being accomplished, if the superior does not change his instructions or order him to stop doing it or modify them in some way, he in effect is endorsing the orders that are in effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that principle, to your knowledge, any different in any other armies than just the VRS and former JNA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly in my knowledge of other armies, and particularly my own army, in that type of situation if the superior officer, the commander, did not modify the instructions, it would be taken as the commander is endorsing the plan of action that has been discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could move on to another area related to the commander's responsibilities. Have you assembled various documents relating to the laws governing the duties of a commander to prevent war crimes and punish war crimes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let's try to, just briefly if we can, go over each of those. I believe the first one you've chosen is P378. It's called: "An order on the application of the rules of international laws of war in the Army of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," dated June 1992 from the Official Gazette. Can you tell us first what this gazette is and what you want to say about this particular document.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in general at the time frame of June of 1992, as what was then known as the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was organising itself into an governmental entity. There was a publication of a number of laws regulating the structure of the armed forces, particularly what we call the Republika Srpska law on defence and the law on the army. As part of that there were also a number of decrees published which, in effect, allowed or directed that this newly established armed force would follow the general international rules and regulations pertaining to the conduct of land warfare. This particular order, published in the Official Gazette, which is the Republika Srpska's legal publication, outlined that the army is instructed to apply the rules of the international law of war, both within the concept of the Geneva Conventions and as well as within the context of a more specified body of regulations published by the former JNA in 1988.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you go through each of the documents you've chosen to illustrate these concepts. The next one I believe is P379.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the SFRY regulations on the application of international laws of war in the armed forces. It was published in 1988 and it is the technical application to the former JNA of the Geneva Conventions as well as the additional protocols that were ratified by the SFRY. In this particular respect I would like to draw the Court's attention to paragraphs 19, 20, 21, and I'll get to some on the next page in a second. Paragraph 20 particularly discusses the issue of individual responsibility for the violations of the laws of war, noting that every individual shall be personally accountable for such violations. Paragraph 21 specifically articulates the responsibility for actions of subordinates. It specifically notes that "an officer shall be personally liable for violations of the laws of war if he knew or could have known that units subordinate to him or other units or individuals were planning the commission of such violations and at a time when it was still possible to prevent their commission, failed to take measures to prevent such violations." The last part of paragraph 21 is also particularly relevant. "An officer shall be responsible as an accomplice or instigator if by failure to take action against his subordinates who violate the law of war, he contributes to the repeated commission of such acts by units or individuals subordinate to him."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would the accused in this case, would their training have, to your knowledge, have covered these specific paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding, in discussing this issue with a number of former VRS officers and VRS officers, is that this is a block of instruction at their higher staff academies at almost all levels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what is the next document that you've chosen in this area? I believe it's P380, the guidelines for determining criteria for criminal prosecution. What is this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document that was published in October 1992 by the military prosecutor's office at the Main Staff, and there's an accompanying cover letter by the commander of the Main Staff that's not attached to this. But what this in effect articulates the policy of the Army of the Republika Srpska with respect to taking legal action against three specific types of crimes. Two of those crimes aren't relevant in this particular case, one of them being failure to be called for service or evading service. However, the third one is relevant because it discusses the policies and procedures by which the army and the military prosecutor are to prevent and investigate war crimes and crimes against humanity under the SFRY law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you go to that section in the document. I believe it's page -- it begins on page 7 of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, this document reflects back to what was then chapter 16 of the SFRY criminal code, and it's interesting to note that this chapter of the criminal code was, in fact, completely adopted by the Republika Srpska as part of the programme of incorporating their own laws in 1993. They essentially just published a decree that the entire body of SFRY law will now be known as the RS criminal code. So this is a body of law that the Republika Srpska has, in fact, adopted. The second paragraph in this particular case notes that "crimes against humanity in international law can be committed by individuals acting on their own. But by their nature, these criminal offenses are usually committed in an organised fashion in the implementation of the policy of the ruling circles. Most of these offenses are committed during armed conflicts or are in some way closely connected with armed conflicts, which means that they are committed within the context of broad military operations and on orders from superior officers."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What other sections would you highlight for the Court?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have a number in this document. The next one is also on page 7 at the bottom of the page. Noting that in this particular case "in addition to preventing criminal acts, which are violations of humane conduct and international law, the armed forces of the Army of Republika Srpska are required to abide by the instruction on the application of the international laws of war in the armed forces," which was the document we've previously discussed. As part of that same paragraph, again dealing with the issue of the superior it notes that following -- "from this follows the explicit responsibility of the officer corps of the Army of Republika Srpska as the giver of orders and commander of the armed forces whose members could commit or are committing some of these offenses to take uncompromising action to prevent such conduct. This responsibility belongs by its nature particularly to high-ranking individuals and officials in state, military, or public organisations who are in the concrete circumstances in a position to issue orders." The next paragraph follows on with that: "If officers merely find out that units of the armed forces of the Army of Republika Srpska or their members have committed or are committing such acts and take no measures to prevent the consequences or the acts themselves and expose perpetrators to criminal prosecution, this in itself makes them answerable for these criminal offences."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, I noted that you in reading that last paragraph, it says that: "If officers merely find out that units of the armed forces of the Army of Republika Srpska," would that include the MUP or is that just the army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the circumstances it certainly does include the MUP as a member of the armed forces, and I would also cite back to the early legislation on the law on defence which particularly notes that the MUP is part of the armed forces. And as you continue to read on and as you go back to the SFRY regulations, it makes it clear that the responsibility of the officer in this case is not limited to subordinates of units under his command, that officer has a positive responsibility under paragraph, I believe it is, 21. It specifies not only of his unit -- paragraph 21 of the regulations on the application. It specifies that it's not only his unit but any unit that he comes across knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next -- what is the next document you've chosen? I believe it's P381. What is this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the decree on the proclamation on the law of the military court system. There's nothing inherently in detail that needs to be brought out in this document, however this is the fundamental document that outlines the military court system of the Army of the Republika Srpska or more accurately of the Republika Srpska in its entirety, and is the primary apparatus by which these charges would be brought through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was there a system in place to punish people who violated these rules related to war crimes and such?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what is the -- what's the next document you have on this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is the law on the implementation of the law of military courts and the law of military prosecutor's office during the state of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is P382/A.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This recognises that in the -- in a declared state of war this document gives expanded power to military commanders to order court martials within the context of their own unit for certain crimes, primarily the disobeying of orders, desertion in the face of the enemy. And where is this is relevant is that on 15 July 1995, the President of the Republic declared a state of war in the Skelani, Srebrenica municipality. Part of that municipality is covered by the Bratunac Brigade, so some of these extraordinary legal powers would have been at the disposal of the commander of the Bratunac Brigade effective at that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So what is the next document, P383.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is dated 16 June 1995, and it is from the government of the Republika Srpska -- in fact, it is from the supreme commander, to all entities of the government. And what it is doing is declaring is a formal state of imminent threat of war. In the Republika Srpska, there were three states under which the government existed, a normal or peacetime state, an imminent threat of war state, or a state of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would this time in June 1995 with the war beginning in 1992 can there have been prior to this decree a peacetime declaration in effect?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For its own legal purposes, the Republika Srpska in November 1992 having achieved what it considered to be its war aims, effectively ended a declared state of war and put itself legally on a peacetime or normal footing. Now, certainly conflict occurred well after that, but from a legislative or legal perspective, the laws and the functioning of the Republika Srpska operate under a state of peacetime rules and regulations. In December of 1994, based on the worsening military situation in the Krajina, a state of war was declared specifically for the zones of the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps. By June of 1995, faced with a worsening military situation country-wide, the government declared an imminent threat of war on 16 June, which gave the VRS expanded powers at the expense of the civilian government in order to conduct the prosecution of the war. And as time goes on, by the end of July 1995 throughout the Republika Srpska, a state of war is declared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the fundamental difference between the powers of the VRS in an imminent state of war and a state of war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are some documents or some regulations which only come into effect during a declared state of war. For example, the last exhibit that we looked at, the law on the military court system in a state of war, it is specific only to that state. For example, those powers of -- those powers of immediate disciplinary action and the power to start his own court martial at that level only applied to him during that state. He does not have those powers during an imminent state of war. So it's a legal clarification to even more expanded powers in some cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which commanders would have those powers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, under an imminent threat of war or a state of war, those powers are delegated down to the Main Staff commander, the corps command, and with respect to immediate court martials, they could be delegated down to brigade and regimental level with the prior approval of the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So what's the next document you want to talk about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a rather lengthy document. I won't be talking about all of it at all, but this is the body of legislation which is known as "The series of laws on ministries during an imminent threat of war and a state of war". This was published on 29 November, 1994, and it is the, as you can note, it is not an open law. It is a state secret. This is the series of laws that would govern the conduct of the government of the Republika Srpska in time of imminent threat of war and a state of war. Specifically in this one there are three issues I would like to highlight being relevant here. On page 4 under the body of law known as the law on implementing the law on defence in case of an imminent threat of war or a state of war, it talks about the issues of full mobilisation of all individuals who are over the age of 16, either in the armed forces or in compulsory work service. And article 10, the establishment of compulsory work units in each municipality to carry out the occasional tasks and to meet the needs of the armed forces as well as other defence needs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is there something else from this section that you wanted to talk about that was relevant to our situation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this body of law, the next relevant situation would be moving further, and it's actually a separate exhibit, since we'll refer back to it as Exhibit 385, which is with respect to the law on the ministry of the interior during a state of war or an imminent state of war. And what this law does is it specifically regulates the use of police units in combat operations as a part of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, going back briefly to our chart, who would this include in terms of police units?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would include the police units under the regional security centres, the CSBs, and it would include the police units of the special police brigade headquartered in the Janja area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I don't think you need to read this out, but can you just paraphrase roughly what it entails and I think we can go over a document to see how it fits in this particular rule.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, article 14 is the important issue that will revolve around the issue of police units coming under the command of the army units in the area that they're operating. If you look at the last paragraph of article 14, in effect it explains why this procedure is so important. As you might imagine, police units do not have the same logistical support or organisation to sustain themselves in combat operation as army units are. Obviously they're not designed to do that. One of the historical problems when you look at the documents in the research on the use of police in combat situations is the fact that they do not have the ability to sustain themselves over the long term, in short they just don't have the logistic support. They don't have medical, they don't have food, water. These all have to be provided by the brigade or the unit that they're operating in the zone of. It is also important with respect to issues of command. This law prevents a police unit from effectively being broken up and having its members placed individually in army units, and it also ensures that by putting the police unit under the command of the army force, that it's going to be treated on an equal footing and that its operations will be controlled by the army and coordinated. And of course in a combat environment that's very important, because all parties to the combat operation have to know what each other's doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to exhibit -- let's keep this at hand, but let's go to Exhibit 386 which is a document the Court has seen before. It's a 10 July order under the name of Tomislav Kovac who we know is the acting Minister of Interior. And can you just first of all briefly tell the Court what this, what this Kovac document is and how it fits in, if it does, with this regulation relating the use of police units in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this document is a practical application of that regulation. In paragraph 1, the police are effectively being pulled from one area of the battlefield and are being sent -- are being directed to be on 11 July in Bratunac. It's designating the commander of the units and it's instructing them when the arrive in the area, and it's instructing the unit commander, in this case designated as Ljubisa Borovcanin, is obliged to make contact with the corps chief of staff, General Krstic. As we go into other documents and we look at the relationship, clearly in this instance when it says obligated to make contact with the corps chief of staff, General Krstic, this is putting the unit at his disposal or being under his command. It follows on from a series of documents that we'll see on the 12th where the army is giving orders jointly to the army and police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, you said being at his disposal or being under his command. Can you clarify that. Are those two different things?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shouldn't say the word "disposal," because it means something different in the JNA parlance. It is, in effect, placing his unit under command of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order for MUP units to be placed under the command of the army, Article 14 requires that police units assigned to combat operations by an order of the commander in chief of the armed forces. Does this July 10th document indicate that there's been such an order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The preamble -- it's not a numbered paragraph, but it notes that pursuant to the order of the supreme commander that the following series of orders, 1 through 5, are being given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let me take you to a practical situation that arose, that the Court has heard evidence on where thousands of prisoners were being assembled along the Bratunac/Milici road on the 13th of July by mostly MUP forces and shipped out in buses and trucks to Bratunac. Would the MUP forces have the logistical capability to have buses and trucks in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, certainly not buses. And any truck transport that they did have would simply be limited to what it would be necessary to move themselves from battlefield area to battlefield area. By design, and particularly in the case of the CSB companies -- or I'm sorry, the PJP companies as part of the CSB, they don't have any of the military infrastructure necessary to do a lot of that type of movement. So all of those resources would have to come from the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who in your opinion would be commanding and controlling those transportation resources in the situation I've described on 13 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my research and the documents that were available, many of them which we will discuss, that was being commanded and controlled by the headquarters of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, that is what I wanted to ask you about on the basic issues of command. Now, if we could go a little further into the rules and regulations related to the conducting of security and intelligence affairs. And have you identified some of the pertinent rules related to that subject?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But first, before we go into those rules, I think you've touched on this somewhat, but can you just give us the barest outline of the chief of security or other assistant commanders or officers in that situation. What basically are the chief of securities and assistant commanders, how do they relate to their command in terms of command responsibility, power to issue orders, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the terminology of the former JNA which is in effect here, those are known as special branch bodies. It acknowledges that unlike the operative staff, these branch bodies are specialised bodies which do specific types of functions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us some examples besides security.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, rear services is an excellent example of a specialised branch body. Within the greater confines of the rear services, for example, you will have specialised organs and officers in charge of a variety of fields to include technical services, which would include ammunition, which would include medical and veterinary support, which would include food services, which would include finances. All of those functions which are part of what a military organisation and a brigade, if we can use that an example, need to successfully conduct day-to-day operations. Yet, it's recognised that an individual who will command the brigade will probably be an infantry or armour or other type of officer, and he will not necessarily be a rear services professional. So while the commander of the unit will have a general knowledge of what those functions are and how they support the overall conduct of the brigade, by virtue of the specific nature of those tasks, he's not going to know the details of accounting, the details of medicine, the details of veterinary, the details of ammunition. So as part of the military system, a series of officers will specialise in these fields through their career. That same principle applies to the security branch. It is a specialised field, and people who are in this field generally have spent a career in this field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, if I could direct you to the, as you've stated, to the brigade level. So what in the brigade level is the title of the -- that particular position?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again depending on the type of JNA brigade, it is considered to be the assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs or a regular brigade, it is the assistant commander for security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's stay with the Bratunac Brigade model, the light infantry brigade. So could you, again, describe to us that specialised branch, how that fits in with the command, the basic duties of that officer.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the security branch is a specialised branch, over the course of the development of the regulations of the former JNA in the past, there are a number of very specific regulations dealing with the roles of the security officer and more importantly the means and methods by which the security officers work within the laws of the greater SFRY. And these are a rather lengthy and arcane series of rules and regulations. Now, a security officer, and certainly the assistant commander for security, by virtue of his position is expected to know in great detail the functioning of that branch and the specifics of the means and methods of work, keeping in mind that the roles primarily envisioned are counter-intelligence and security of the general forces. Now, again the commander will have a general idea certainly of what the security branch is and does and how it incorporated within his brigade, but the commander is not going to have the detailed knowledge of the means and methods and the regulations specifically used by the security officer in the conduct of his daily affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can you define for us simply -- we've heard this word "counter-intelligence," and it has all kinds of potential layman's meanings, but can you define for us the term "counter-intelligence," as it's meant in the VRS context and then we'll go to the next body of responsibility of the security officer.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the VRS context, counter-intelligence is again a broad category by which they label the means and the methods which they use to ensure the greater security of the unit that they're assigned to. It encompasses two particular areas, if you will. In the first area it is what other countries would call "counter-espionage". Those types of measures to prevent an enemy force from learning details about the particular unit. Counter-reconnaissance-type of operations, operations to prevent the enemy from gaining intelligence information or battlefield information about the unit, operations to prevent members of that particular unit from passing information to the enemy. And in another sense, it also relates to the issue of protecting information, military, confidential, or state secret, from either the deliberate or inadvertent exposure to the enemy that could be of use to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't mean to interrupt, but given that we have this definition in the context of which the gentleman put it, if he could tell us for the record where did he get this definition from or was it something that he derived from his general knowledge from reading the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, the witness is giving testimony. And if you have some questions, you could raise it during your cross-examination. But of course we come to this juncture. If you think it's feasible, Mr. McCloskey, you could ask this question so that we could have a whole picture of that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. As I'm sure you've seen, I try to start off with the general so we can understand generally what the picture is and we go to the regulations and get the more specific and then we will have actual examples of counter-intelligence orders. So I'm getting there and we can keep going in that direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for counter-intelligence, Mr. Butler, we haven't gotten to the regulations yet, but there are definitions of counter-intelligence and discussions of counter-intelligence in those regulations, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just briefly, in these sorts of counter-intelligence operations, does a security officer have his own assets that he can use separate from the corps or the brigade, excuse me, let's stay with the brigade.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally the assistant commander for security will have one or two subordinate security officers that work to him to assist in the accomplishment of this task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's stay with the Bratunac example and Mr. Nikolic. What did he have in this time period? I think you've already discussed it, but can you just remind us.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the case of the Bratunac Brigade, the other officer who was assistant, who was also designated as an intelligence officer was unavailable. I believe Mr. Nikolic had indicated he had one former non-commissioned officer who assisted him in some of the administrative matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said counter-intelligence was one responsibility of the security officer. What was the other?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the other responsibilities: It is envisioned is he also functions as a law enforcement arm of the brigade as well. He has responsibilities under the regulations for criminal investigation and for the conduct of supervising the activities of the military police. As it was designed within the JNA regulations, they saw criminal prevention and security as very closely related fields, and in many cases overlapping. So in that particular aspect, it makes sense to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the security officers particular command relationship with the military police in the Bratunac Brigade at this time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the Bratunac Brigade at this time, it was, in effect, as prescribed by the regulations. The assistant commander for security supervised the daily functions of the military police, he recommended the most appropriate use of the military police to the commander, and it was up to the commander to either accept that recommendation or to make changes according to the events that were occurring on the ground at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did the security officer have absolute control over the military police platoon in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, he would not have had absolute control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us examples of the practical day-to-day operations prior to Srebrenica what the military police would be involved in in relation to the security -- well, to Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the things that most occupied the time of the military police when they weren't actually conducting combat operations was the functions generally associated with law enforcement. Particularly in the Bratunac area and a lot of cases, this meant being tasked to go out and apprehend service members who had left their units without authorisation and to bring them back to their unit. You would also have within the Bratunac Brigade the military police were assigned fixed checkpoints, one of them being just outside the Srebrenica safe area perimeter at a place called Zuti Most or Yellow Bridge. You would also have a manned police station or a police desk where the military police would be available, and again that would be the focal point for the conduct of law enforcement activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the military police, who was his direct superior?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: His direct superior in terms of command would have been the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, with that general background, let's go into -- have you identified the rules that were most applicable for the conduct of security affairs in the brigade, such as Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've identified a series of these former JNA documents which are applicable. With respect to the command of security organs and the supervisory or professional chain of communication, the most applicable one is the rules of service, which is Prosecution Exhibit 387. With respect to more general terminology on the means and methods of that work and on intelligence support to the armed forces, there were other regulations that are incorporated in my revised narrative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Before we get in particular to some of the sections of rules of security service, as you've stated before it would be Momir Nikolic's job to be not only -- he was the chief of security and intelligence. So what again roughly would his intelligence responsibilities be and how did that relate to security responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to intelligence responsibilities, by regulation, the responsibilities are to take the necessary steps to organise the gathering of reconnaissance information, intelligence information, defector or prisoner of war report information, to analyse it, synthesise it, and report it up through the chain of command to superiors. He is, in essence, the person responsible to the brigade commander as well as reporting up to the corps on the intelligence and reconnaissance-related issues that are occurring in the Bratunac Brigade zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's go to what you wanted to point out to us for the rules of service for the security organs. And again, if you could just highlight what you feel to be some of the most significant, and I'm sure you'll be prepared to talk on anything in particular on this subject.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This chapter 2 of this regulation delineates the differences between command of the security organ and the provision of specialist administrative services or professional support to the security organ. Paragraph 16 specifically notes that "the security organ is directly subordinate to the commanding officer of the command, unit, institution, or staff of the armed forces of whose strength it is placed in the establishment and it is responsible to that officer for its work." The next part of that sentence deals with the JNA security organs in the larger former ministry of the interior and national defence and generally aren't applicable here. Paragraph 18 notes that the security organs of the superior command, unit, institution or staff of the armed forces provide specialist administrative services for security organs in subordinate commands, units, installations, staffs of the armed forces, provides assistance to those organs, and organises, directs, coordinates and supervises their work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the professional tasks of the security branch within the former JNA, in this particular case within the VRS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professional task being what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those professional tasks would be things related to counter-intelligence or counter-espionage operations. Those types of very specific and arcane tasks which the security officer is mandated to do by the regulations and are best given to him by security officers at a higher level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That seems to conflict with the previous paragraph 16 where the security officer is -- must come under his -- the command of his commander. Can you explain in a little more detail what kinds of relationship the, for example, the corps security officer has with the brigade security officer that is outside the competence of the brigade commander, if any?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are some relationships that the corps security officer will have that will be outside of the competence of the brigade commander with respect to professional tasks. One of the things that has to be noted in the context of the former JNA and the VRS is that many of these regulations are also again designed within the framework of the environment of the former Yugoslavia in the mid-1980s. We are not talking about a democratic state for nature, we are talking about a country whose security rules and regulations were designed at a time when there was a totalitarian power or communist party in charge there. So many of these regulations have a fallback position to allow for the security branches to monitor events that are occurring in the units, in part to ensure the complete reliability and the complete fidelity of the unit commander. Now, as time goes on through the 1980s and certainly by the 1990s when the VRS adopts these regulations, you do not see that particular political aspect in existence anymore. However, that same channel is used as a reflection of the fact that in many cases, battalion and brigade commanders can be seen as the targets of either a counter-espionage investigation themselves or as the target of a law enforcement investigation that would run under the auspices of the security operation -- of the security branch. So those are examples of where the system is designed that the object of investigation, should it be the commander, that there is a way to conduct this investigation without the commander's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll see some examples of that a little later on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about in the work related to working with the military police in the detention and handling of prisoner affairs which you discussed earlier. Does the corps have any special relationship outside the commander in that area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that particular instance, the relationship is not outside of the command or the commander. The security branch by regulation and by the commander's direction is the branch that is responsible for many of the aspects of dealing with prisoners. However, it is also recognised within the JNA rules that it cannot obviously strictly be a function of the security branch. Particularly with the conduct of prisoners and prisoners of war, there are a lot of other things that have to occur for their safeguarding. So while the security organ can ensure that the military police can safeguard the prisoners, and while the security and intelligence organs can begin the initial intelligence interrogations of such prisoners, it is recognised that other branches of the brigade in this case are going to have to be brought in to the process, to help to secure prisoners with respect to a facility to secure prisoners or to feed the prisoners, to provide for medical assistance to the prisoners, to provide for their movement from the initial holding point to future holding points. So while the security branch in this respect is the branch that so to speak takes the lead in this issue, the issue of prisoners cuts across a lot of different staff sections of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And can we go to, I believe, paragraph 23 in these rules as well. Can you briefly synopsise what that's about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This talks about the relationship between the security officer in a particular unit and his management function over the military police of that particular unit. It notes "he recommends to use of the officer to the command, unit, institution or command, and he is responsible to him for the state and activity of that unit." Again that is a technical supervisory function. When we look at the practical aspect of that, as Mr. Nikolic has testified, he does discuss the issue of making recommendations to the commander on their daily use or on their use for specific tasks, and it is up to the commander to either approve those recommendations or to modify them as he sees fit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Is there another -- what was the next -- did you want to say anything else about those particular rules?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think we're ready to move on to the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what else did you want to say on this subject? I believe it's P388. And what is this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the 1985 service regulations of the former SFRY pertaining to armed forces military police. If you look at paragraph number 13, it is again a restatement of the roles and responsibility of the security officer as we've just seen in the 1984 security regulations. It notes that "with respect to speciality, the officer in charge of the security body of the unit or institution controls the military police. He makes suggestions to the officer in charge of the unit on their use and is responsible for the combat readiness of the military police unit and the performance of its tasks." However, back to paragraph 12, it specifically notes that the officer in charge of the military unit and institution to which the military police unit is attached commands or controls the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, we have another document that was recently identified by Ms. -- by the defence of Blagojevic from one of the voluminous collections of the Prosecution. It's P389. This document is dated October 1994, and it is under the name of General Mladic. It appears to be signed -- well, it's hard to make out the signature. Is this a document you had heard about prior to it actually being provided to us by the Blagojevic defence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document that in general terms we knew to exist. In the case of Radislav Krstic, it is a document which the Defence knew existed in general terms as well but neither the Prosecution or the Defence were able to come up with. So in general terms, we knew of the existence of this document. Specifically as the Defence in that case had noted that it was something that they felt exculpated their person. For us, finding this document was always a rather high priority as we recognised it as something we would have to deal with under Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what efforts were made to identify this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally on my part and on the part of a number of assistants who work for me, a great deal of man hours and days were spent searching through various databases in an effort to come across this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was it finally found by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was found in a collection of over 125.000 scanned electronic documents, which were provided by the SFOR in Bosnia when they searched two facilities, one of them the former Zvornik Brigade, one of them a brigade in Brcko for violations of weapons storage procedures under the Dayton Accords. When SFOR searched these facilities, they seized all of the documents, they made electronic scans and at the request of the Office of the Prosecutor, we obtained a copy of the electronic scans. We did not obtain the original documents. This particular document comes from one of the documents that was seized by -- or that was taken from the brigade that was searched in Brcko, which is in the Bijeljina area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you actually make efforts to scan that collection in an electronic search capability?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We made considerable efforts, the first effort being an 18-month process with my assistant analyst, Ms. Brettell, and the people working in the OTP software service to actually develop search capabilities for this system. When we originally received it from SFOR, all we had was essentially a number of CDs with scans on them with a very limited search capability. So for the first 18 months of the process, our people were designing prototype search tools necessary to scan this collection in both the Latin language and the Serbian Cyrillic language which of course complicated things. Once the search protocols were installed, we certainly realised that on any given search that we were looking for we were only getting 50 or 60 per cent of the hits available because of the quality of the scans themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you had looked at each one of the thousands of documents individually or printed them all out and looked at them individually, I take it you would have come across this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eventually we would have come across it. It would have been at the tail end of the search, because I can honestly state that given the priorities at the time, looking for documents that came out of a search in Brcko would have been the last priority as opposed to looking for documents that came out of Zvornik. So ultimately we would have come across it, but had we started that process a year or two ago, it would have probably been next year when we found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this came out of the Brcko collection?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This came out of the documents from Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Setting all that aside, let's get to the document itself. What is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document which is the -- which are the instructions for how the head of the security organ of the VRS and how the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic, wants the security branches within the army to function. It is a series of instructions which detail to commanders and to security organs what part of their work, they're going to do and which part of their tasks that they're going to focus on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it provide anything of major import or anything new that you recognise or different?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many of these part which are restatements of the 1984 security regulations and the following armed forces intelligence regulations. But one of the things of specific note is in paragraph 1, where the commander of the Main Staff is directing that the VRS security and intelligence organs spend 80 per cent of their time or 80 per cent of their resources engaged in intelligence and counter-intelligence tasks and they should only spend the remaining 20 per cent involved in administrative responsibilities, military police oversight, and criminal legal tasks and duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that's probably a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And just for the record, this document has also been previously marked D22/1 in the Defence version of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, you -- before the break you pointed out what paragraph 1 said, basically as it says, dividing the tasks 80 per cent and 20 per cent. And those were divided along the lines of tasks that you already have described. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. How about paragraph 2. What can you tell us about that? I note that it starts off with: "The security and intelligence organs are directly commanded by the commander or the unit or institution of which they form part."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where does that come from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is again out of the regulations for security organs, again reflecting the fact that the organ is commanded by the commander, but with regard to professional activities, they are controlled essentially by the security intelligence organs of the superior command. The next sentence makes it clear that they have full independence in the implementation of intelligence and counter-intelligence tasks and operative combinations, based on the authority set forth in the law and the authority of the appropriate superior organs. One thing I would like to note in this particular instance is: I would like to check the translation. If this in fact is accurate and it is "law," we don't have a copy of this law. So I'm not sure exactly what it is. If it is regulations, then they are referring back to the service regulations which we've already discussed. So that's one thing I want to highlight up front. If it's a separate law, it's not a law that we have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've already discussed briefly the counter-intelligence work as you understand it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And paragraph 3, what is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 sets the framework that obligates all members of the armed forces, the VRS in this case, VRS institutions commands, and other members to provide assistance to the organs in the realisation of their intelligence and security tasks and to not take any actions which could endanger those type of tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What else in this document do you find of significance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, paragraph 4 again refers back to the rules of service and the instructions on applying work and means of the intelligence organs of the VRS. Those are clearly referenced back to regulations which we have, and noting that this is how these operations are to be performed in accordance with those rules. Paragraph 4 also notes the fact that with respect to the intelligence and counter-intelligence reports, that the telegrams and mail in this respect are delivered exclusively to the security organ, and that no other organs of the command, including the commander, have the right to inspect their contents. So it creates the inviolability of the communications channel between the superior organ and the subordinate organ in this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why would that be necessary in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the broader sense in the intelligence and security world, and as it's certainly noted in the JNA rules and regulations, that intelligence and security matters are generally regulated, and the knowledge of them are regulated on a basis of need-to-know. Part of that type of operation is the fact that generally the more people who are aware of an operation, the higher degree of compromise, obviously. It goes back to the point where in some cases brigade officers or potentially the brigade commander may be the target of an investigation, and, clearly, if the brigade commander or his staff are aware of that, that's going to handicap the ability to do that investigation adequately. Moving to paragraph 5, this clearly regulates or sets out the protections that a security officer has with respect to his contacts with the brigade commander and with respect to the superior officer of the security organ above him. It notes that, for example, that VRS units and institution commanders who have members in their ranks may be consulted on matters pertaining to decisions on transfers, appointments or assignments, and that they may recommend, make proposals, but they cannot in effect take their own action. Again, reflective of the special circumstances of the security branch, where these individuals cannot be automatically transferred or moved by the brigade commander without at least clearing this through the superior chief of security. It also notes that unit and institution commanders may pronounce stimulative measures, punishment or other measures for these members only with the obligatory consultation of the first superior in the service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in a practical sense and again reflected on a lot of the VRS documents from 1992 to 1995, it's not unheard of where commanders will attempt to retaliate against security officers who have reported on them in some means of nature. This is a means of mechanism by which security officers can be protected. It means that before the commander can take any disciplinary measures or otherwise, he must be able to justify those measures to the next in the chain of command. It would be the security officer at the higher level and also presumably the corps commander in this particular case. It also designates that the chief of security and intelligence organs are, by functional task, the nature of the work, members of the collegiums and commander's personal counsel of their unit. It's restating the fact that commanders cannot, whether they trust their security officer or not, they cannot isolate the security officer. They have to recognise that the intelligence and security officer is a key component of his core staff and needs to be wrapped into the process. And the last one is that the recruitment is carried out in according to the criteria defined by the headquarters of the Main Staff security and intelligence sector, and that they are the only ones who can recruit members of the security and intelligence branch. Going to paragraph 6, instructing security and intelligence organs and units and institutions to provide assistance in their work to the 410th Intelligence Centre and the VRS Counter-intelligence Group, consistent with their work as well. I mean, again mandating the security officers have to deal with other security organs as well. Chapter 7 places the onus on the superior security officer to monitor the professional correctness of the work of the security organ, except for the part of their engagement relating to the command and staff affairs. That professional supervision and that command remains under the purview of the unit commander. And finally paragraph 8, instructing all commanders and other officers to adhere to these and noting that the instructions should be forwarded to all commanders and units at battalion level. And battalion level is the lowest level you see an officer designated as a security and intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you -- what do you make overall of this document as it relates to this situation in our case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this particular case, I mean the key thrust of the document is clearly the statement that the Main Staff is trying very hard to ensure that the bulk of the work that the security officers do are dedicated to what they perceive the most important tasks of the security officers, the intelligence and counter-intelligence functions. As a lot of these security officers engage in law enforcement activities, and many security officers were sent because of their experience as line commanders to command units. And this is an attempt in these instructions by the Main Staff to limit that practice as much as possible and have these trained assets to focus specifically on the areas to which they're trained. One of the interesting things to note about the commander's ability to remove these officers while in isolation it appears to be a significant degradation in command. If you look at the rules and regulations in effect in the Republika Srpska army specifically in the ministry of defence, the ability of a brigade commander to remove his own officers is already somewhat limited. Depending upon the position function and the rank of the position in question, many of those appointments are already limited to the minister of defence or the commander of the Main Staff in making those changes. So it's not really that big an event that a brigade commander is informed that he does not have the singular authority to remove one of his subordinate officers. That is similar in other cases as well depending on the rank position of the officer in question. And those are all regulated in the army law and the special instructions published in 1992 by the RS minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The security officer's at the brigade level dealings with the military police in the detention and housing and interrogation of prisoners fit into the 80 per cent counter-intelligence side of this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reading of the rules and regulations and particularly the intelligence and counter-intelligence piece, most of those functions would not fall strictly within the 80 per cent. In the counter-intelligence and espionage functions, they would with respect to interrogation of prisoner of war and intelligence issues, while intelligence falls into that, those tend to fall outside because they are issues that the commander is involved in with respect to needing to know the intelligence information. And certainly it specifies that issues pertaining to oversight of the military police fall outside of that 80 per cent and fall strictly into the lesser duties of the security officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Have you been able to identify some documents that show a practical application where brigade commanders are working with and reporting on the work of security branches?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let's go, I think the first one is Exhibit 390. Can you tell us what this is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the reporting regulations of the VRS, units were required to publish an annual report, and in some cases a semiannual report concerning the combat readiness of their unit. This particular document is a report of the combat readiness of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade for the period 1 January - 31 December 1994. As a component of this report, if I can direct your attention to page 11, paragraph 6, the brigade command starts a rather lengthy explanation on all of the activities in a general sense that are being conducted by the intelligence and security organ of the brigade. It lays out the strength of the organ, what the organ is missing, and further on page 12 discusses issues pertaining to training. In paragraph 6(A), it discusses the issues of intelligence support. And in paragraph 6(B), it discusses in detail issues of security support. And by their own definition, they're identifying the type of work that is given to what they call counter-intelligence work; these are the tasks which they consider. And some of the examples that they give: The confiscation of radios from Serbian individuals to prevent them from talking to Bosnian Muslims across the lines. The protection of military weapons from thievery was considered a counter-intelligence or a security related task, while it was also related to law enforcement. It talks about issues where cases of one soldier in the zone of responsibility had direct contact with the Bosnian Muslims, and that once the security organ found out about it, they took the steps to prevent that. Notice that all data collected by counter-intelligence work is duly delivered to users. Again, still under security, it discusses the roles and activity of the brigade military police company and what it is doing in its role up over the year. And more along the lines of the relationship between the security organ and the military prosecutor and military court. And in the last paragraph, a general assessment by the brigade command as to the work of the security branch and how they see the future going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what does this indicate to you regarding the involvement of a commander in security affairs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This typifies the broad knowledge that the commander and the command in general have on the functions of the security organ in the Zvornik Brigade. As you might expect, you do not have specific information where the security officer of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade is putting in this document how many informers are members of his unit or where they were located. You do not have specifics, since this is an annual report, you will not specific pieces of intelligence placed in here. But what this reflects is the fact that there is a general awareness on the part of the brigade command, what the roles and responsibilities of the brigade security and intelligence organs are as a member -- as a part of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go to the next document. Were you able to find a Bratunac Brigade document along the same lines?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It is listed as Prosecution Exhibit 391.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you get this document from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was seized by the OTP during the search of the former Bratunac Brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you put on the ELMO so we can see whose name is on there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it possible to scan out, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The machine will scan up, I believe. It's an A4 document. There we go. Thank you. So what is this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As discussed before, recording the requirements of the VRS, this is the Bratunac Brigade semi-annual evaluation of their combat readiness for the first half of 1995. It's dated 4 July, 1995, and it, of course, is sent to their superior, the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's under the name of Mr. Blagojevic, dated 4 July. How long had he been -- just remind us, how long had he been the commander at that time.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Blagojevic assumed command of the Bratunac Brigade on 25 May 1995. So he has been the commander for two and a half months at this point roughly. And as you can see from the original, this is the original B/C/S version, and he has signed this report. If I can direct your attention to page 6 of the English language translation, just like the Zvornik Brigade report, this also has a section pertaining to intelligence and security support. And noting that the security branch is -- for the most part is devoting most of their time to intelligence and counter-intelligence tasks, pursuant to that October 1994 instruction from Main Staff. It notes that the training of the staff, that they're planning courses for battalion security organs. It notes in the next paragraph one particular instance where the brigade does not have an established sabotage and reconnaissance platoon, as a result of well-known reasons. In this particular case, that platoon known as the Mungus platoon effectively deserted en masse and showed up later in the Serbian Republic of the Krajina as mercenaries under the ministry of interior of Serbia. So they mass-defected in this particular instance, as far as we can tell from our material. It notes the reconnaissance squads are being formed in all battalions. It reflects the fact that they themselves in their communications platoon do not have equipment to intercept the radio communications of the enemy, but that they're working with the corps radio reconnaissance platoon in order to intercept equipment working at the VHF frequencies. It talks about "the engagement of intelligence and security organs and reconnaissance uses collecting information of which decisions on the use of our own forces can be made successfully and on time." Clearly, the practical application of this information being collected is going to the disposal of the brigade command and brigade commander for use of his tactical decisions. Counter-security-related issues: They're working very hard to prevent communications via Motorola so the enemy doesn't intercept their conversations. The last paragraph in this page specifically notes that the military police platoon is engaged as planned on orders of the brigade commander. And the training was also planned and completed in accordance with the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. McCloskey, one question. Before you leave this document, you said that Colonel Blagojevic became the commander of the Bratunac Brigade under 25 May --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. There will be an exhibit which indicates that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: This document is for July. For me, it's not two months; it's one month and a half at most.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I'll take that into account.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not your first mistake, is it Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I suspect it won't be my last. Continuing with this document, there's a slight break in the paging, again noting the activities of the military police platoon, and continuing on in that same topic, it also reflects some of the issues and problems of military police platoon. One of the things of interest here is it notes that during 1995 that the military police had the responsibility of monitoring the passage of the various international organisations as they pass through or stayed in the brigade's area of responsibility. This, of course, the travelings in and out of the Srebrenica safe area. And it reflects that this information is monitored and that every significant event was reported to the superior organs of the Drina Corps and Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. So here clearly a situation where the brigade command might not know the exact details of each and every one of those reports that Captain First Class Nikolic has sent up to his superior organ, but they are well aware that he is reporting to those people. And the final observation in this one, how they evaluate themselves with respect to their performance of their tasks, "particularly from analysis of the work done in the last six months, we concluded that the intelligence and security work in the brigade has improved and that all intelligence and security records are in good order." So again, not specific details of what those intelligence and security records are, but a general awareness of the records themselves, what they contain and what type of order they're in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could just go back briefly to page 8 where you mention briefly the fourth paragraph down, the brigade's area of responsibility, a checkpoint was established for the control of all international organisations. Can you relate that back to any orders that you have previously discussed relating to international support for the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what this will relate to, I don't believe we've discussed it yet, but what this will relate to will be supreme command directive 7, which discusses what the role of the Republika Srpska armed forces with respect to the monitoring and later the actual conduct of trying to prevent international organisations from fully accomplishing their duties. In this particular case, the checkpoint that they are discussing will be the military police checkpoint established at Zuti Most or Yellow Bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's my mistake. I realise we haven't gotten to that document yet. All right. The next exhibit, 392. It's listed as a command of the Drina Corps security department to various commands of various brigades, strictly for the chief of intelligence and security affairs. And it is under the name of Vujadin Popovic. Can you tell us what this is and why you've chosen to discuss this document.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there has been a lot of discussion in a number of cases over the types of information that may or may not be withheld from a commander by a security officer. And I chose to discuss this document because I believe it is an excellent example and one of the few that I know exists, certainly within the OTP, of a document that it's fairly simple to conclude that this document would not have been shown to the commander or his relevant staff officers and would have been maintained only by the chief of intelligence and security affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So tell us -- we don't want to read the whole document, but can you tell us what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular instance, the Main Staff intelligence and security branch has obtained information which indicates that the assassination of General Mladic and General Tolimir have been ordered by some members not designated.
