And what this document does or what this order does is it directs that during visits to the area, security officers will ensure adequate physical security and counter-intelligence security, and they will also establish an investigation, each security officer will begin investigations in their own unit to try and determine if there is any information which could assist in the investigation in this respect. It notes specifically that they are to inform the security organs in their unit, their own security referent and the subordinate battalions on a need-to-know basis in order to collect information related to this case. It notes the security file that's going to be opened and it gives instructions for passing the information that's received and instructions on what to do if you actually come across the individuals who are part of this conspiracy. It also notes that all information on this subject will be reported by mail, again to ensure security, that it isn't compromised through normal telecommunications channels or it isn't inadvertently leaked to another staff member. So this is what I would view as a classic example of a document from the security department of the Drina Corps that would go to subordinate security officers that by necessity the brigade commander and his staff would not be made aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The secrecy and the nature of this document, would that relate to a security officer's duties with the detention of large numbers of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it has nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we can move from security, unless Your Honours have any questions on that, any further questions, we can go and discuss some of the issues related to the duties of the Zvornik Brigade chief of engineering. And can you briefly describe for us -- you've already pointed out where that person fits in the structure, but can you briefly describe what kind of a job that is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In many respects, the chief of engineering services, while they're considered part of the operative organs of the brigade staff, because engineering is an operations-related function, it is recognised that engineering services are a specialised field. To give an example, it would probably be the same in the case of air defence, anti-aircraft defence forces. It is part of operations but it is a specialised field. The role of the engineer officer on the staff is to provide that professional technical advice and suggestions to the commander as to the use of the engineer assets in that unit, once the commander approving them or modifies them, it is his job to take the commander's directives in that part and ensure that they are carried out by the subordinate engineer formations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say ensure they're carried out, how would a chief of engineering ensure they are carried out? What authority does he have?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like other staff officers, he's operating under the delegated authority of the chief of staff and the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so what can he do?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the regulations indicate, he has the ability to task those units that are directly under his staff supervision with respect to regulating their professional activities. A practical example would be while the brigade commander would order a series of bunker emplacements to be built at a certain location, it would be the responsibility of the engineering staff officer to determine which units of the engineer company would best do that, what orders have to be given to ensure that the resources are available to be there, that the fuel is available to be there. Those type of technical issues which a commander by definition would not normally have the time or the technical expertise to get into the details of. That is the classical role of a staff officer on a staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that include issuing instructions to the engineering company?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us a bit about the engineering company and how it relates, if it does, to the chief of engineering.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the engineering company in many respects is exactly like the military police company. The engineering staff officer is responsible for all of the professional and training aspects of that organisation. However, the engineer company commander falls under the direct command of the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us more about the engineer company in the Zvornik Brigade for July 1995, roughly how many people, what kind of assets it had.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the engineer company, and we will get into the details on this later, as we have the actual breakdown roster for July 1995, consisted of approximately 70 to 90 individuals broken down into three platoons. One of them heavy equipment road construction, one of them general engineering, one of them what we call pioneers or combat engineers. They had more equipment than most units, but certainly not engineer-related equipment to meet their own needs. One of the things that we'll see in this regard is that a lot of the equipment they're using has been requisitioned from local industry. For personnel and manning, the engineers like a lot of the other formations of the military were short on qualified individuals. In July of 1995, for example, the company commander was an individual by the name of Dragan Jevtic who by professional was a civil engineer. He was not a professional military engineer. A lot of the other platoon commanders were of the same background. They had an engineering background, but not necessarily a military engineering background. So in that respect, the staff officer who was an engineering staff officer had additional oversight, and in many instances directed the activity of those platoons and that company because of their lack of military engineering experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Dragan Jevtic's direct superior?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his direct superior in a command sense would have been the brigade commander Colonel Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let's go to the exhibit you've chosen for the engineering unit. I believe the first one was P393. Can you tell us where you got this document and what it is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a definition -- I mean, this is the rules on the utilisation on the rules of the SFRY and this is a document that the Office of the Prosecutor did not have and was provided by Defence counsel for Mr. Jokic. It is like many of the other things that we've seen already, it is the SFRY rules on engineering and the utilisation in the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't go too fast. I'm -- we need to keep it slow, but keep going.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we've seen in the cases of other officers, by regulation their general duties and functions are specified. And I believe since the Court has seen this, there are only a few issues I would like to point out. The last paragraph on the first page again reflects that "Pursuant to the commander's decisions, coordinating and consulting with organs of the command, it proposes tasks of the engineering units in terms of priority, makes a plan of engineering security, prepares orders for engineering security of the subordinate combined units and as well as directly subordinated and supplementary units."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just make sure the record is clear, it reads "cooperating and consulting".

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, "decisions, cooperating and consulting". Again, and noted on the second page the third bullet, "controls execution of tasks issued to subordinate engineering units, provides the units with necessary expert assistance and monitors effectiveness of employment of engineering units and material and technical resources." Again, going through these entire series of roles, the classical statement of a staff officer on a brigade staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says: "Controls execution of task". In a practical sense, how would the chief of engineering control a particular task and what authority does he have?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from a practical standpoint, in most cases the commander of an infantry brigade is not going to be a professional military engineer, present exception noted in this case with the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell the Court what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my understanding that Colonel Blagojevic is, in fact, a military engineer. But in the case of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, Colonel Pandurevic is an infantry officer and Lieutenant Colonel Obrenovic is an armour officer. So these individuals are not going to have the detailed knowledge of all of the steps and procedures necessary to adequately supervise an engineering project. That responsibility or that task is going to be delegated by the commander and the chief of staff to the officer on the staff who has the training and the ability to do that, in this case the engineer staff officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to the job in -- that's referred to as the brigade duty officer. Now, we've heard a fair amount about that already, Mr. Butler, but can you just give us your very brief outline understanding, based on the documents you've read, about what that job entails.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The specific in this instance, the brigade duty officer is a rotating job that each of the officers qualified in the brigade assume on a 24-hour basis. The duty operations centre is manned on a 24-hour-a-day, seven-day-a-week basis. It is a continually functioning organ or internal organ of the brigade command post. Officers are placed in this duty based on a roster by the chief of staff. This office, by its design, is the focal point where all information impacting the brigade and their combat-related activities passes through. So it is, in effect, the nerve centre of a lot of the information which comes in and out of the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What, in particular, are the responsibilities of the brigade duty officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can direct the Court to Exhibit 394. Again, this is the manual for the work of the command and staffs. Page 34, starting at paragraph 64, it discusses the duty operations officer and at 66, his specific duties. It makes it very clear that the duty operations officer is a very, by regulation, active participant in things that are occurring that are of importance to the brigade, the monitoring of combat operations, particularly the second bullet: "To inform the commander and chief of staff about any major changes or orders issued by a superior which require a decision of the commander." To the third bullet: "To be familiar with the disposition of the elements of the command post and to know the locations of the commander, chief of staff, and assistants to the commander." Further on: "To make sure that control and communications are maintained with superior and subordinate commands." It further calls for the receiving and dispatching of orders and reports to other organs which they not be able or off shift at the time. To monitor and verify measures for the immediate security and defence of the command post and sound alert in case of attack. And in that last paragraph, it discusses all of the documents and plans which the duty operations officer must have in order to do his work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it says to receive and dispatch orders, can you describe what that means.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a practical manner, the functions of command mandate that the commander and frequently the chief of staff are going to be out among the actual forces. I mean, certainly the commander will, that's his place to be is with his troops. In recognition of that fact that there will be times when the commander is not physically at his command post, that when orders come in from the superior command, as they will be passed to the superior duty operations chain, or by direct telephone contact from the superior command, it is his case to make sure that those orders are implements and to keep his commander informed of those orders when they need his decision. Some orders can be independently implemented by the duty officer. The bulk of the orders that the duty officer receives are in fact orders that have to be passed on to his commander because they will require a commander or chief of staff decision. But it recognises the fact that the duty officer -- if the commander and chief of staff are not available for whatever reason or out of communication, the duty officer -- it is within the purview of the regulations for him to take the initiative and make the orders that are required to fit the combat situation at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When a brigade duty officer such as Major Jokic receives an illegal order from above, such as to make arrangements for the detention and killing of prisoners or the burying of prisoners, what are his duties -- excuse me, under his rules, what are his responsibilities in responding to such an illegal order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, the regulation goes back to -- this one is the 1988 regulations on the applications of the law of war. It clearly specifies that no officer or no soldier is under the obligation to follow an order that they recognise as being unlawful at face value. Regardless of any other tenet of the regulations, if the officer can recognise that the order is unlawful, he is not obligated to carry it out. And again, as a position, as an officer and a person of superior responsibility, granted not a commander, he is obligated to take steps in order to ensure that the violation or the order for the violation is reported up the proper chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would the duty officer's responsibility be if he merely passed on that order for others to carry out?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, going back to the SFRY instructions on that, just passing it on he becomes part of that process. And those are regulated in those paragraphs. We can go back and look at them specifically. The Court and obviously everyone has those. You become part of that process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the brigade duty officer, is he more than just a switchboard person passing on things? What is his responsibility, really?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can refer back to the document here, paragraph 65. And it notes that the operations duty officer and his assistant commander are commanding officers in the command. In this respect, they're not talking about individuals who are actively battalion or commanders or brigade commanders of that nature. What they're talking about are officers who are qualified to command and lead formations. These are experienced, seasoned officers because this is recognised as an important duty, particularly given the absence of a commander or deputy commander as the circumstances occur. This is not a function that they're going to give to junior officers with no experience. They may very well be assisted, but it is recognised that the operations duty officer when he's on is considered to be a representative of the commander and that the people who are performing this duty are, in fact, the most qualified officers in the formation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's switch gears a little bit and I want you to be able to give the Court some of the basic background information that you have learned about, first, Colonel Blagojevic. Can you briefly summarise what you know about his background.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the VRS background of Colonel Blagojevic, we do not have that many documents which would assist in laying that out; we have a few. I will detail through them just to give a quick synopsis of what information we do have on his background and where we have received that information. If I can direct the Court's attention to Exhibit 395, this is the translation of an article from a VRS military magazine called Drinski magazine. It was first the military magazine of the Zvornik Brigade and later became the military magazine of the entire Drina Corps. On the third anniversary of the Zvornik Brigade, it gives a rundown of the former brigade commanders. I would highlight for the Court that where it notes "three years have passed since 02 June 1990," as printed, clearly in this instance, the magazine misprinted that and it's 1992, as it notes in the first line. But, of significance, it notes that the first commander of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade was established was Lieutenant Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how long he was the commander there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my understanding that he was not the commander there more than a month, month and a half. As you go through the article, he is replaced at a point in time by another JNA officer. And at that point in time, I don't know where he goes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know Mr. Blagojevic was a JNA officer before being in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we've had a number of individuals who have told us that again Colonel Blagojevic was a professional JNA officer. He is not a reserve officer. He has his rank as a basis of his former status in the JNA as an active service officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What else do you know about him from the document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next glimpse, it's probably the best word to use in this instance, of the tracking of the career of Colonel Blagojevic in this respect is an order published by the Drina Corps to the Zvornik Infantry Brigade detailing reserve Lieutenant Colonel Bosancic to assume the position as the acting chief of staff of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. And this is dated 28 October, 1993. At the bottom of that order under that explanation it reflects that the present acting chief of staff of the brigade, Lieutenant Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic, is to return to his previous duty at the corps command, so another person must be appointed to ensure the proper operation and functioning of the brigade staff. This indicates that during some period in the fall of late summer or early fall of 1993, Colonel Blagojevic performed the duties as the acting chief of staff of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't know for how long?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Where I start to get an accurate picture of Colonel Blagojevic starts when he assumes command of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade on 25 May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is Exhibit 397. Can you explain what this exhibit is, what this document is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, and we will see more of these types of documents, as part of their reporting requirements, brigades were required to submit a daily regular combat report to the superior command, and in this particular case being it's the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, that superior command is the Drina Corps command. This is the daily reporting mechanism by which the brigade command and specifically commander reported the activities of his unit to the corps command, specifically for the corps commander. Paragraph 2 of this particular document notes that the transfer of duties was established -- took place at 1000 hours under the supervision of Major General Zivanovic. And while it does not specifically note him as being appointed as the commander, he signs the document as the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, as is the custom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a signature?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular document, all I have is the electronic version. So while we have the typed, signed signature, we do not have his actual signature like we saw in other documents. In many of these documents and as we'll get to them later, we will actually have the handwritten draft of these documents before they were typed into message form, and you'll see a variety of signatures, some of which will be his on these documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's go to briefly what you know about the background of Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document P398 is the English translation of a document found in the professional military personnel file of Dragan Jokic during the OTP search of the Zvornik -- or the former headquarters of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. This reflects all of the pertinent information on one sheet pertaining to then-Major Jokic. At this particular time when this document was done, he was listed still as Captain First Class. It notes his branch as in engineer. It notes his current duty assignment in the VRS is the chief of engineering of the brigade. And moving further down, it notes one of the interesting phenomenon which we see with officers of the former JNA, those professional officers, and how their pay and other related forms of military subsistence and administrative support are regulated through the 30th Personnel Centre of the Yugoslav Army General Staff. One of the things we will see consistently when we look at VRS officers who are from the former JNA and who are active serving officers, is they will hold a duty appointment in the VRS and you will see that on line 15 and they will also hold what I call a shadow appointment within the VJ, the federal army of Yugoslavia, and you notice that on line 14.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did Mr. Jokic begin the chief of engineering job based on this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm having trouble reading off the monitor. Let me just go ahead and ... It notes - again, it's a handwritten notation - that he assumed the position of chief of engineering on 6th December, 1992. And of course, it also notes in line 12 that he had actually been in the VRS since 16 May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you have another document related to Mr. Jokic and the engineering -- well, excuse me, related to Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, and because of the lines it's not showing up well on the monitor, obviously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: P399 for the record.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is the English translation of the log which tracks the presence of - in this particular case - the officers and soldiers of the Zvornik Brigade command in July of 1995. If you note line 13, that indicates that Major Jokic is the chief of engineering of the brigade, it is his duty in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it says Major Jokic NINZ, how do you know what that means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What will be the limit probably of my ability to understand the Bosnian Serb language, N is the abbreviation for "nacelnik," which is chief. INZ is engineering. If I can then note, this is the actual Bosnian Serb language of the chart, noting again on 13, Major Dragan Jokic and this of course shows where he is accounted for on each and every day of the month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what those little pluses mean next to his name?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Going back to this, the English language translation, as a part of this log, the person who filled out this log put an index as to what the place names and what the codes are. A plus indicates that they are present for duty. There are other codes that you will see, SL or C equals off. T is a reference to on the terrain or in the field. You have references for sick leave or hospitalised. You have references for AWOL. You have references for if they are attached to a battalion. And of course T is noted twice in this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't see a plus. How do you know plus, what that means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In interviewing a number of individuals about this log, we were informed that plus is the sign that they use to indicate present for duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is so they wouldn't leave the spot blank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this document shows Dragan Jokic present for duty from --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we can scan up just a bit it will be clearer. This is 13, column is him. And we scan along. It shows the period on the ELMO now from 1 to 23. And it shows that with the exception of the 13th, he is present for duty -- I'm sorry, I think I'm on the wrong line. With the exception of 12th, he's present for duty. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now I want to switch gears again, and if you could provide us a brief historical outline of the events leading up to July 1995, some of the key events, and then, of course, we'll get into some of the documents that lead up to the attack on the enclave.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without going into too much on the broader context of military operations in the Drina valley or the Podrinje region, it's fair to say that as part of the creation of the state of Republika Srpska, there was a lot of military operations involved in various parts of that what later would become the Republika Srpska. With respect to the Podrinje area, after initial takeovers of various municipalities by the local Bosnian Serb forces, the Bosnian Muslim forces begin a series of counter-attacks and over the ensuing months of 1992 greatly strengthened their hold on a lot of that area. In some effects the Bosnian Serb forces were almost limited to the major populated areas of that region which is known as Lower Podrinje. In a greater sense, the Republika Srpska army chose to allow that to happen because a more significant and critical issue for them was to control the Posavina corridor area in the northern area from Bijeljina towards the Krajina. At a strategic level, they understood that if they could not secure the Posavina corridor during the summer months of 1992, there would be no chance for them to ever have a viable state. By August, September, and moving into October of 1992, the army of the Republika Srpska by and large achieved those military goals. And then began to turn towards now securing the rather precarious hold they had on the Podrinje area. One of the first manifestations we have of this - and it's a document I'll go into some detail in a little bit - is the directive for further operations, or what we call, Supreme Command Operational Directive Four, which lays out in macro terms what the goals and objectives of the army were. Now, one issue to note in this particular case is that in November 1992, the Drina Corps is established as a corps entity in the Bosnian Serb or VRS army for the very first time. That's significant in so much as the fact that while the VRS used former JNA corps headquarters that had left the country as the nucleuses for their own corps as they were formed, the Drina Corps had no such advantage. The Drina Corps headquarters was organised essentially from scratch. And it was organised on 1 November 1992, when it became clear that the collection of other units and other corps that covered that zone prior would be militarily unable to conduct operations and to secure that area. So in effect, the creation of the Drina Corps represents, you know, the Main Staff of the army and the supreme command now focusing on the critical area of the Podrinje valley. I think in this context, the UN report provides an adequate background as to the military and political events which lead through 1992 to the establishment of the safe areas in the summer or May, spring of 1993. So I won't go into those in too much detail. That status essentially remains until January of 1995. In January of 1995, as I've discussed earlier - let the interpreters catch up here for a second - the strategic balance seems to be shifting away from the Republika Srpska and towards its adversaries. And despite the ceasefire that's in effect in January and February, certainly the VRS understands that that cease-fire will not last and that offensive operations by their adversaries will begin in the spring. This leads to the publication of the Supreme Command Directive Seven and the version of it, 7.1, which in effect note that the issue with the enclaves is now coming to a head and that a permanent solution for these enclaves has to be effected, because manning around the enclaves is now more critically needed in other places. So that is the broad overview which brings us from the Podrinje valley campaigns of 1992 to the spring of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we start getting into the documents now. Perhaps it's a good time to take our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, after your brief synopsis, historical synopsis, I want to take you back now to the time frame, I believe it's November 1992. You mentioned a directive. Let's start to go through the documents that will help with the outline you've just given us. So if you could take the document you've chosen, I believe it's Exhibit 400. Tell us how that fits into what you'd told us before. Tell us what it is, first of all. And could we -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is what is known as directive for further operations of the Army of Republika Srpska or what we call operational directives. In this particular case it's operational directive number 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is an operational directive?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: An operational directive is a political military document which in effect lays out the long, intermediate, and short-term goals and war aims of, in this case, the Republika Srpska. So these documents are very useful, particularly for me, in being able to look at one document and see where the political objectives are outlaid and how the plan is to accomplish them militarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you get hold of this particular document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, and I believe all of the strategic directives or operational directives that we have were seized by the Office of the Prosecutor during the search of the headquarters of the former 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what does this document tell us relating to what you had begun telling us about before?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in paragraph 1, and I won't go into detail on this, since you can read it down the line. But I mean, within that context it outlays what the Bosnian Serb military view is of the overall war situation. And it discusses what they believe the Croatian aims are, what they believe the Bosnian Muslim aims are and as the course of the document will go down it will outline, in general terms, what the Army of the Republika Srpska plan to be. Now, specific to campaigns related to the Drina Corps, if I can invite your attention to page 5 of that document, the paragraph D if I can get it on the ELMO correctly. This specifically outlines the goals and directives of the Drina Corps in context with the overall political objective. And if I can read it says: "From its present positions, its main forces shall persistently defend Visegrad to the dam, Zvornik, and the corridor, that's the south end of the Posavina corridor, while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region shall exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him, and force him to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas together with the Muslim population. "First, offer the able-bodied and armed men to surrender and if they refuse, destroy them. After that, unblock and repair the Konjevic Polje/Zvornik road, make it fit for traffic and stand by for intensive combat against infiltrated sabotage, terrorist, surprise and ambush attacks, and paramilitary groups." And finally it designates to set up a command post in Vlasenica and a forward command post as decided by the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is there any problem or anything wrong in terms of the Geneva Conventions to exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him, and force him to leave the area of Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that context, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the next line, together with the Muslim population. What do you think that means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it indicates to me that the overall objective of the attack is to force the Muslim population out of the region. That is not something that is supposed to be able to happen within the contexts of the Geneva Conventions. So as I look at this, this is -- my impression is what we're looking at is generally an unlawful operation as described to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have a map -- we just provided you with a map, 364. If you could just point out again, just to remind us, where Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde are.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Birac is this region right here in and around Sekovici and in here. The Zepa area is here. And the Gorazde area is here. So in effect, what they're calling for is the depopulation of most of the area within the zone of the Drina Corps of the Muslim population. Now, what has not been noted in this specific order is the eastern portion of the Drina Corps zone, known as the area of Romanija has not been specified. But by November of 1992, the Romanija area was predominant Bosnian Serb, so there was not a significant Bosnian Muslims population in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Continuing with this document, if I can draw your attention to the last page in English, page 7 noting that this document was drafted by Major General Milovanovic. Again, as the chief of staff of the Main Staff and signed by Lieutenant General Ratko Mladic, the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What's the next document you've found relevant for this period?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we move forward to 1995, the next document that is relative with respect to the safe areas in Eastern Bosnia is directive number 7. And this was published on 17 March, 1995. And again, coming off the cover sheet, that's Prosecution Exhibit 401. From the supreme command of the armed forces, state secret, and in the same context as operational directive 4, the first series of paragraphs outlined the political military context as perceived by the leadership of the Republika Srpska. So when I make that characterisation of what I understand to be the strategic situation, in a large part, this is what I'm basing it on, the perceptions of the Republika Srpska government, as articulated in these documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Like you did before, can you go to the section related to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can take you to page 10 of the English translation. This is the task of the Drina Corps. It notes that: "Enemy breakthroughs along selective operational tactical lines should be prevented by extremely persistent defence in cooperation with the forces of the SRK," and that's the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, a neighbouring corps, "and on the north-west part of war front around the enclaves. As many enemy forces as possible should be tied down by diversionary and active combat operations on the north-west part of the front, using operational, tactical and camouflage measures. While in the direction of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, complete physical separation of Srebrenica and Zepa should be carried out as soon as possible, preventing even communication between individuals in the two enclaves." And the last sentence: "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that last sentence, can you relate that in any way to the directive from November?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you couple it with the directive 4 from November 1992, it's a continuation of the longer-term policy goal that the Republika Srpska is not willing to tolerate a sizable Bosnian Muslims presence in Eastern Podrinje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is there anything else in this section that provides any information about that process of creating a situation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, moving to page 11, part of that same paragraph it specifies that: "In case the UNPROFOR forces should leave Zepa and Srebrenica, the Drina Corps command shall plan an operation named Jadar with the task of breaking up and destroying the Muslim forces in these enclaves and again definitively liberating the Drina valley region." Moving to page 14 of the English language translation, there's paragraph 6, support for combat operations. The fourth paragraph notes that: "The relevant state and military organs responsible for work with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations shall, through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits, reduce and limit the logistic support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources to the Muslim population, making them dependent on our good will, while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the international community and international public opinion."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you relate this to a previous Bratunac Brigade document you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've mentioned previously, in the semi-annual report of the Bratunac Brigade, there was that phrase which indicated that the work at the checkpoint at UNPROFOR was proceeding in accordance with the plan of the Main Staff and also the brigade commander. So in connection with those two, you see the practical application or the actual manifestation of part of this plan. The last piece of this document, page 15 of directive 7 again notes: Drafted by Colonel Miletic, who was at this time, he is the chief of operations of the Main Staff, and it is signed by the supreme commander, Dr. Radovan Karadzic. And this is the B/C/S signed version of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So as we move ahead from March 1995 towards July 1995, is there a document that's -- excuse me, there's another document that's related to that one you've just mentioned, P401, and that is P402. Can you tell us what that is and what the significance of that is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This particular document, given the very large-ranging goals for the entire army in directive number 7, in this instance the Main Staff published supplemental directive 7-1 or 7/1 in order to break up those goals into more manageable pieces for the military in terms of time and objectives. This document was published by the Main Staff. With respect to the Drina Corps, it takes the broader objective that is listed in 7 and puts it into more appropriate military terminology with respect to the sequence by which military operations will take place, indicating that the first task in coordination -- I'm sorry in corporation with the IBK, and in this instance, IBK is the Eastern Bosnia Corps, that's the corps to their north, is the complete task from Operation Spreca 1995 as soon as possible. It would then work to continue the other tasks in directive 7. This takes into account that at the time operation 7.1 -- this directive is being published, they are in the middle of Operation Spreca 95.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Spreca 95 was a VRS operation designed to counter offensive operations by the Bosnian Muslims 2 Corps in the Majevica and the -- in that greater Majevica area. And that was primarily within the East Bosnia Corps. But because the Drina Corps was the corps just to the south, particularly the Zvornik Brigade was significantly involved in components of that operation as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything else you find significant in this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 6, support for combat operations. It notes that: "Through planned and coordinated information and propaganda activities with state organs and media institutions, exposed the bias of UNPROFOR and the international community, which are allowing the enemy to arm freely and continually attack Serbian defensive positions from the protected zone of Tuzla." In, effect, is part of the Spreca 95. Now, what else is significant in this document is probably best defined by its omission. In directive 7, we had the language with respect to Srebrenica and Zepa that they're to create situations where the population has no hope of survival. That language is absent in directive 7.1. Also in directive 7, you had the directions with respect to the plan to create the conditions where UNPROFOR could not properly supply the enclaves. That language is also not present in directive 7.1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what do you make of the lack of those two dramatic bits of information in the previous directive?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assessment is that again, reflecting that operation directive 7.1 is designed to cover a shorter period of time and be more specific to the corps, that given the focus of the events occurring in March and April of 1995 in directive 7 and 7.1, that language wasn't included because it wasn't relevant to the operations that were occurring in those separate months. Clearly we see operation -- we see the language in operation 7.0, particularly the strangulation of the UNPROFOR forces in the enclave manifested in the activities. And I believe a number of UN people have testified to the situation there over the months of January to July. So clearly we see the effects of operational directive 7, even though it is not specifically specified in 7.1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as we move up towards July to the period of the actual attack on the enclave, is there an another relevant document you've chosen among this group?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context, since as a course of my research for this trial we were focusing primarily on the issues with respect to the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, one of the more relevant documents that we have, the OTP came in possession of through its seizure operation in Bratunac, is a book where the minutes of commander's daily meetings or select commander's daily meetings were noted down, and we call this the meetings and report book of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. This book is fragmentary in so much as it does not have notations for every single day, and in some cases it skips notations by month. But there are relevant notations for the period of late June and July of 1995 that provide insight as to the working operations of the Bratunac Brigade, as well as insights into the effectiveness of command and control of that period. I start here on page 2. This is simply the commander's observations at a meeting on 28 June, 1995. And just looking over it, it just demonstrates very simply nothing more than effective exercise of command. The next one of significance will be page 4 on the English language translation. And this reflects the 30 June 1995 meeting with the commander and brigade command. And again you'll note, some of the more routine items on the agenda. The semi-annual analysis which we've talked about earlier, courses for the battalion, and one thing it does note of interest, or at least interest to me, is that this notation that the chief of staff of the Drina Corps with the staff visited the brigade zone of responsibility, the 3rd Infantry Battalion. The 3rd Infantry Battalion with its headquarters at Pribicevac ultimately becomes the main access of advance or avenue of the attack, if you will, by which the operation of Srebrenica takes place. So this indicates to me that this is the first visible piece of planning by the command of the Drina Corps in the operation which would be known as Krivaja 95. Moving to the next page which is 1 July 1995, page 5 of the English translation. This affects 1 July 1995, again reflects meeting, the commander, chief of staff, assistant commander for logistics, morale. The practical application of the issuing of orders and the staff reporting compliance of past orders. These are the normal functions of a brigade commander and his staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't see the chief of security at this meeting. Can you -- do you have any reason why he wouldn't be there or do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is not a chief of security listed there, and it does not specifically say. However, if you look down under assistant commander for operations and training, it does say Nikolic. So I don't know what to make of that particular thing. The only thing I do note is that Nikolic, Captain First Class Nikolic is the only Nikolic that I'm aware of on the brigade staff. This is a particular lengthy one starting on page 6 of the English translation. And what we're now getting into the time frame when the Drina Corps is publishing the operations plan, Krivaja 95, for the reduction of the Srebrenica safe area. This reflects a broader meeting between the command staff and the commanders of the battalions, all four battalions and the worker's battalions. And the commander is present at this. And again the practical application of a commander and his staff going battalion by battalion, and becoming aware of all of the relevant security and personnel and logistics issues within the framework of the area of responsibility of his forces. And on page 7 of that, it continues, where we discuss issues or where they discuss issues of the 4th Battalion, the commander of the workers battalion. Major Nikolic talking about with respect to what lies ahead. So further about what to do with rifles that were taken away, his suggestions. And then continuing on in page 8 to the end of the meeting, what all of the other staff people are doing, Major Eskic, his chief of personnel, Captain Gavric, the chief of artillery. Major Trisic, the chief of the rear. And then the commander's guidance at the back. That last notation: "The battalion commanders will stay with me and the chief of staff, and the rest of the staff is dismissed." So while nothing of significance jumps out, this is a practical demonstration of a brigade commander in effective command of the brigade. The last two notations on this go to 4 and 5 July, and again reflecting that at this point in time the brigade command and its core command staff are now becoming fully engaged with the Bratunac Brigade's role in the upcoming operation against the Srebrenica safe area. And it notes particularly that they've read out the order from the chief of staff of the Drina Corps for full combat readiness of our unit, also preparing the work for the brigade command, and some other things that have to be resolved, the status of the former workers battalion, and it also notes that you need to prepare a plan for the engagement of the command staff in the units. And we'll see bits and pieces of that further in the future. And on 5 July, the last meeting of this series in the notebook, again administrative orders pertaining to the visit of a unit of the Bratunac Brigade deployed out of the Drina Corps zone in Trnovo. Instructions to Nikolic to provide a public address system and interpreter and select a place from where the address shall be best heard from Potocari village. It notes that he's telling his staff exactly where he's going to be, "I'm going to the 3rd Battalion zone." Micic, who is a lieutenant and operations officer at the Bratunac Brigade is to go to the 2nd Battalion zone and do what we agreed with respect to collective weapons. And to clarify for the Court, if I can, "collective weapons" is what we in the U.S. military parlance would call crew-served of weapons. Those are weapons such as mortars, recoilless rockets, types of military weapons where it takes two or three or four persons to operate. It notes that the chief of staff will go to the 1st Battalion to increase accuracy in the direction of artillery fire. And that his other staff officer Eskic will go to the crew of a 20 millimetre anti-aircraft cannon. And where this is significant to me is that it highlights one of the techniques that a commander at any level will use to ensure that his subordinate commands are fully cognizant of what the orders are and that they will be complied with. And that he sends members of his staff down to those subordinate units in order to monitor the activities of those units. In this case, Colonel Blagojevic is directing his staff officers to go to the subordinate battalions where they will monitor the activities of those units. And this is something that we'll see in the continuing days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about this reference to Nikolic to provide a public address system and an interpreter to select a place from which the address shall be best heard in Potocari village. Do you have any idea what that's about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only from what is listed at the face of the document itself, that Potocari village at that time is under the control of the UNPROFOR forces, headquarters UNPROFOR battalion is there, and there are some Muslims living there. But I don't know the specific details of what that's supposed to imply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the last notation at this time continuing 5 July, 0730 hours, is the brigade commander presented the order of the Drina Corps command to presumably his command at the time. And that was all that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have that order from the Drina Corps command regarding the attack on the Srebrenica enclave, the Exhibit 543. Now, we don't want to go over this entire exhibit, but can you tell us from your analysis, what can you point us out to of importance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again the date published, 2 July 1995. This particular order came out after our previously published preparation order to get forces moving. But I will try to focus it on the relevant aspects for the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, if I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, does this document cite any previous documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As indicated in paragraph 2, it is referencing the operations directive number 7 and 7-1. So it's using that as its base directive to -- as the planning foundation for operations to split apart the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica, reducing them to their urban areas. And that, again, is the goal reflected in directive 7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you -- what does it mean by reducing the enclave - let's talk about Srebrenica - to its urban area. Do you have the map that will give us an idea of the enclave and its urban area? That is Exhibit 364 -- actually, that's not the one I was thinking of. The one that actually has the urban area. Yes, that one. This is Exhibit P85. If we could blow that up, focus it on the Srebrenica area. If we could zero in on that a little more -- no, I'm sorry down. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this gray line is the outline of the border of the Srebrenica enclave. This small little switchback in the road here which you can see, the brown doesn't show up unfortunately too well on the monitor, is the actual urban area of the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the rough sizes of the urban area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as -- based on the geography primarily, it is in a very narrow valley. So I think the rough size we tend to use as a working rule is 1 kilometre wide by 2 kilometres long. And that is the urban area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where do the population of the enclave live?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A good chunk of the population of the enclave lives in the urban area, however, there are also a number of very large settlements, particularly towards the south end of the enclave here. One particular settlement of note for displaced Bosnian Muslims is the Swedish shelter project, which is a refugee village, if you will, under a Swedish NGO, where 5.000 people are living. So there is a substantial Bosnian Muslim population in a lot of those southern villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what do you think reducing the enclave to the urban area means? What effect would that have in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've testified to this extent in the Krstic trial, the practical effect of that would be to replicate the conditions that existed in early May 1993 before the UN designated that as a safe area. A situation where you had a very large humanitarian crisis, where you had 30 to 40.000 people pushed into an area and you did not have the life support functions necessary to sustain them. And as a result of that humanitarian crisis in May, the UN initially attempted to evacuate the Bosnian Muslims out of that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say May, you mean May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: May of 1993, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you've already spoken briefly about the separation of the enclave from Zepa. I don't think we need to get into that again. So --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Continuing on, it's page 4 of the English language translation. It starts talking about projected offensive tasks for these units. Now, in this particular case, and one of the things I'd like to clarify in advance, is you will see the acronym first BPR, and you'll also see first BLPBR. To clarify, when you see the acronym first BPR, the unit they're referring to is the 1st Birac Infantry Brigade. When you see the acronym first BLPBR, that is the acronym for the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. So in this case the instructions to other units of the 1st Birac Brigade and the 2nd Romanija Brigade, and then further down instructions to the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade and where they're going to conduct offensive operations. Turning to page 5, it talks about reserve forces of the Drina Corps being comprised of two or three companies of the MUP and one company from the Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade. In this respect I only highlight this because at the beginning of my testimony in the case of Krstic, when asked my opinion on these reserve forces, it was my understanding at the time that these were part of the special police brigade from Bijeljina. As noted later in my testimony in the Krstic case, the investigation came to learn of the existence of these PJP companies subordinate to the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. And we've also come to learn that those, in fact, are the companies that were designated as the reserve, not the companies of the special police brigade in Janja. I just want to clarify up front when we talk about the reserve companies with respect to Krivaja 95, we're talking about one or two of the PJP companies from the Zvornik CSB, as well as one company from the Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I notice it says for the reserve forces to prevent an enemy withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a traditional role for reserve forces under a commander. One of the things that was anticipated was that the enemy would withdraw rather than become actively decisively engaged in Srebrenica and that additional forces might be required. The police forces since they wouldn't be engaged in active combat operation made the type of forces that you could ideal assemble and put anywhere on the battlefield without disturbing other operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the police forces end up -- that did come later to assist this operation, what did they actually end up doing, just very briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in fact they did just that. They were deployed along an axis which the enemy was withdrawing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 6 of the English language translation, it designates the combat security intelligence functions on page 6, and then later page 7, the security functions. And again, for intelligence, making it clear that information is to be gathered and that it will be available for the commanders and units engaged in the attack. And in paragraph -- on page 7 under security support, talking about again the more traditional counter-intelligence function in security, preparing the conduct of the operation work out, coding documents, and take care of documents to make sure they are not compromised. It also indicates that the security organs in the military police will be indicate areas for the gathering and securing of prisoners of war and war booty. The next line is that dealing with prisoners of war in the civilian population, they will behave in every way in accordance with the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those sections is the corps commander taking any responsibility for prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In effect, the corps commander is directing that the security organs take these measures. So he's giving that authority or he is giving that authority to the security organs as the professionals to regulate that. He is designating it as the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does that give up his responsibility by delegating the authority?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it does not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What else, if anything, in this document do you think is of interest in understanding the situation as we approach the attack on the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one thing on page 9, just in communications, command and communications. Communications readiness and the requirement to submit daily reports. Again, part of the broader command issue of verification that orders are being carried out and the results are being transmitted up to the superior command. The corps command expects to be fully informed on what's happening in this operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It also says, designates the forward command post in the Pribicevac area. Can you -- if you could get that map out again, and if you can show us where that is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Srebrenica, and literally going uphill from that, you will find a small -- very small village called Pribicevac. And this is where the forward command posts were designated for both the Bratunac Brigade and the forward command post of the Drina Corps for this operation. As part of the continuing reporting process from the Bratunac Brigade to the Drina Corps command, the Bratunac Brigade on 4 July is providing the situation to its superior. It is noting its forces are at high state of combat readiness in accordance with the corps order. It notes the brigade commander visiting artillery firing positions, and the chief of staff is visiting positions of the 2nd Infantry Battalion. Now, this particular report is one of the ones where we have the handwritten draft version of it before it was put on the teletype machine. And while this is a handwritten one, and this is the teletype one. And where the significance is here is that on these teletype messages, you will of course not see the physical signature of the brigade commander if he signs the document. All you will see is a notation from an individual who the investigation understands is a communication clerk of the Bratunac Brigade at the time. And I should also note that the investigation also understands that this individual has passed away. But going back to the handwritten document, here you will see the physical signature, in this particular case a signature which I understand to the Colonel Blagojevic's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you think it's Mr. Blagojevic's signature?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As previously indicated on a number of documents and a number of documents which we were not going to tender specifically as exhibits here because they're not relevant to court proceedings, there are documents, orders, promotion orders, things that are signed only by the commander. And in reviewing all of these documents over a number of years, I have come to recognise myself that this is his signature. What you will normally see and we will see on a number of documents, is that if another officer signs for the commander, and officers are delegated to be able to do that under circumstances, you will see in this area here the letters z-a, za, indicating that the signature is for the commander and it is not the commander's signature. And when we get to some of those examples, I will of course point them out, sir. This document now is a document that I believe the Trial Chamber has seen, P406, which is the Bratunac Brigade order for active combat operations with respect to Krivaja 95.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where did you get this document from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document originally came as a Defence exhibit. I understand that the origins of the document are somewhat unclear as to where it came from. All I can say is it does not have an Office of the Prosecutor ERN number on it, so I'm not able to track it back to any of our documents. Having said that, in examining the document in detail, with what I could do with respect to analysing the document and how it interrelates with other material which we know, it is my opinion that what we are looking at is an authentic document itself. There is nothing wrong with the document from that regard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And just to be clear, you say it doesn't have an ERN number on it. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the practice of the Office of the Prosecutor that every document that is in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor has a -- or any document that we take from any witness or search or seizure, anything that could potentially be an exhibit before the Court, for accountability purposes is stamped with an ERN number. If I can go back very quickly to the last document, P405, just for demonstrative purposes, this number here is what is called the ERN number. The document will have an ERN number in its original B/C/S form as well. So for accountability purposes, back to 405, on the electronic version the ERN version ends in 4515. The handwritten version ends in 4517. And the back page of the document was also placed in and ends in 5416. The final piece of that is as we go back to the English language translation, not only does the Office of the Prosecutor ERN as evidence the original B/C/S version of the document, it also ERNs as evidence the English language translation of it. And this is the mechanism by which the Office of the Prosecution tracks material through its possession for accountability purposes before the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the electronic SFOR collection where co-counsel Tomanovic found the October security instructions, they don't have ERN numbers on, do they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They do not have a classic ERN number, they have what we call a DA number on them. In order to ensure the accountability of that collection, what was done as part of the processing of that collection was that each of the scans was electronically printed with the numbers that begins with the letters DA. So each scan has a DA number associated with it and that is the mechanism we used to track that. Because of this number, once the document that had come up earlier, the 24 October document arrived at my desk using that number that indicated it was DA, we knew instantly that it was a document that had been in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor and we were able to track it back to the collection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Be that as it may, whether or not all the numbers are correct, can you tell us what you find important on this document for your overall analysis.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one of the things that I find important is if you look at the first page of the English language translation, it discusses the deployment of the 28th Infantry Division, the Bosnian Muslims forces in the enclave. And one of the things we see here is that this text is almost a direct lift from the intelligence situation as published in the Drina Corps July 1995 op plan for Krivaja 95. This is actually a common practice in the VRS and one we will see later in our own documents where they will just take blocked paragraphs, if you will, from the document of the superior command and republish it as its own. On page 2 of this document, after the intelligence overview, the commander designates the tasks of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. That task being for the most part to defend decisively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you -- just for the record this is Exhibit D17/1.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But moving to paragraph 4, it is where specifically the Bratunac Brigade commander begins to delegate the tasks out. It begins with his statement of what we in a western military parlance would call the commander's intent. The commander sets out his intent of the operation on behalf of his brigade. Now, while for the most part the Bratunac Brigade has an active defence role --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean? We keep hearing this over and over again, decisive defence, active defence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: An active defence role in this instance is different in so much as a passive defence. An active defence is to conduct the operations necessary to keep the enemy forces who are in front of you engaged with you. It doesn't mean go over on the attack, but it means that you cannot sit there passively. You are to do the things necessary to keep the enemy forces engaged against you in contact with you. Clearly from a military perspective, what no one wanted to happen was that once the operation began on the south-eastern side of the side of the enclave, that Bosnian Muslims forces engaged against Bratunac Brigade units along the more north-eastern side would disengage and be used to reinforce. So this active defence is a military operation designed to keep those forces fixed in place so they would not be able to reinforce other areas of the battlefield. Now, as well as that, the 3rd Battalion was given another specific task of preparing and conducting with auxiliary forces an attack along a significant axes, the Pribicevac, Olovine, Kvarac, and Divljakinje - I apologise for the pronunciation - axis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Keep it slow, especially if you're going to mispronounce words.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. And in fact, this is a supporting attack designed to complement the larger attack being conducted by other units of the Drina Corps. In paragraph 5.6, the commander designates his reserve, that being that, if necessary, have the military police platoon ready for deployment in the sector of the command post of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is using the military police platoon for reserve normal, from your review of these materials?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the SFRY regulations, it is not a normal use of the military police platoon. With respect to the practical reality of warfare in Eastern Bosnia in July of 1995, the military police were very frequently used in combat operations. It's a reflection of the shortage of manpower, and again it highlights the fact that while the assistant commander for security can recommend and even disagree with the use of the military police platoon, the police platoon belongs to the commander and he uses it as he sees fit under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as you've stated before and as this Court's heard evidence, there are significant numbers of the 30 military police platoon soldiers have permanent assignments at various places, guarding Zuti Most, the headquarters, other things. Can you tell -- militarily, does this order anticipate that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding of paragraph 5.6 is that not that these people will be withdrawn from their current assignments. What it is is that these people can continue their current assignments, but if necessary they need to be prepared to deploy from the headquarters of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade in response to the commander's direction. This is what in my military background we would call a be-prepared order, to stand by to do this, but continue on with your normal activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If they get pulled as reserves, what happens to their normal duties?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their normal duties get set aside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What else in here do you think is significant?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, paragraph 10 with respect to intelligence support, in many ways it echoes the fact that intelligence is to be conducted on these axes and the information provided. It provides for reliable guides to every platoon. It provides for protection of cryptographic materials at all levels of command. And it designates where prisoner of war and war booty will be collected. In this case it is to be taken to Pribicevac. It further directs that all forces will comply with the Geneva Convention in the treatment of prisoner of war and the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What significance do you hold the commander's statement regarding prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, two issues in this one. One, it is the commander who is directing where the prisoners will be assembled. And this makes a certain amount of sense, given the fact that the operation commanders will be at Pribicevac. By directing that the prisoners that are taken during that part of the operation be sent there, it ensures that any intelligence from those prisoners can be rapidly used by the military commanders. It also is his personal direction that in the case of prisoners of war, they will comply with the Geneva Convention. This order applies to his subordinates. So as a broader level, this is a commander designating a command function. He sees the issue of treatment of prisoner of war as a command responsibility, not a security one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was dated 5 July, 1995. Have you seen any evidence indicating that Commander Blagojevic no longer took responsibility for prisoner of war on the 12th, 13th, 14th, 15th, 16th, 17th, 18th, 19th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't see an abdication of that command function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anything else in this document of significance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can turn to page 6 of the B/C/S version, again noting the commander's signature and the official stamp of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I note there's a stamp here. Does that -- do you notice any za in front or under that stamp in any way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be appropriate for anyone else to sign anyone else's name or copy the commander's signature on such a document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the general framework of certainly the JNA and in most militaries, forging your commander's signature is a significant offense. Certainly given the fact that officers were designated to be able to sign for the commander on certain issues, there's no need to do that. If the document required the commander's signature and couldn't be signed by the commander, the chief of staff or the deputy commander was normally in power to do that. Certainly minor staff functionaries would not be signing the commander's name for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last thing I'd like to bring out on page 7 of the English language translation, again, is the reporting requirement. Again, for his battalions to forward their daily reports of the situation and interim reports as necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where does that fit into your analysis, just to remind us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are proper and diligent exercises of the command function. Since we raised the issue of prisoners of war, I would again invite the Court to turn back to the regulations on the application of internal law of war on the armed forces of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 407.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where issues pertaining to prisoners of war are discussed on page 60 of the English language translation. Now, many of these, and I don't need to go into them in detail, because for the most part they are direct lifts from the Geneva Conventions. What I would draw the Court's attention to are those provisions found on page 63 of the English language translations, which discuss the issues of the beginning of captivity of a prisoner of war. These are found in paragraph 213, 214, 215, and 216. And in this it is codified by the Geneva Conventions and noted in 207 under the basic rights of a prisoner of war, it notes that these rights and privileges to be granted are not those of an individual or those of particular units.
