They are ultimately the responsibility of the authority of the detaining power. And in practical terms, the armed forces is the executive agent for the detaining power with respect to prisoners of war. It specifically notes that individuals are not the property of the unit necessarily that captures them. The fact that a prisoner of war is taken in one specific unit does not relieve other formations or other people from the responsibility for their proper detention and their proper care and their proper transportation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're referring to paragraph 207?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And finally, the last sentence: The responsibility does not rule out the personal responsibility of individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you note anywhere in these rules the process or an ability to turn prisoners over to civilian authorities, such as civilian police or other civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rules in this particular case do not specify a procedure that turns them over to a civilian authority. The general practice, at least as far as the SFRY is concerned, is that prisoners of war generally remain in the custody of the armed forces. Armed forces in this case being the army, and on limited occasions, the Ministry of the Interior police forces. When you look historically at the pattern of prisoners of war in the Republika Srpska, you see that manifested in so much as prisoners taken by the army, they're moved by army means of transportation, and certainly in 1995 the military prisoner of war detention camp in Batkovica is controlled by the military. So the entire chain of custody for prisoners of war in the practical sense is a military chain of custody for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is the military prison in Batkovica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military prison in Batkovica is located just to the south-west of the Bijeljina area in the zone of responsibility of the East Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's just several kilometres north of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is approximately 15 to 20 kilometres north of the boundary between the Drina Corps and the East Bosnia Corps. Probably about 35, 40 kilometres from the city of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Anything else you wanted to note about -- Well, let's go down to -- well, is there anything else you wanted to note about this law relating to prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not a law. It is the regulation for international law, and again my wider point is these are direct lifts from the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you just briefly summarise for us what the -- 216 is about the personal belongings of prisoners of wars.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a military sense, property on a prisoner of war is delineated in two fashions. There's military property and there's personal property. Military property in this sense would be his weapon, certain parts of his military equipment, whatever types of other military-related equipment he would have, and that of course becomes war booty of the capturing state. Personal items belonging, and it is in effect specified here in paragraph 216, include first and foremost clothing, food, personal protection, and in this sense it would be his helmet and any other protective-related material that he's wearing, his identity card, personal correspondence, and family photographs, and things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And briefly on interrogation, maybe one last question, in interrogating a prisoner, how important is it to have ID documents related to that prisoner and why?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, going back to the JNA manuals on the work and means of intelligence in the armed forces, you're required to have the identity documents, notwithstanding Geneva Convention requirements to identify the prisoner, but because as an intelligence official that is one of the ways you would verify information that the prisoner is telling you that he would have a means of knowing that information. One of the first steps in any interrogation, and we will see that in future documents, is the identification of the individual providing the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it might be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
